Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

derivations.claim: Multiplying $(\omega-\omega^3)(a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3)$ and reducing every power $\omega^j$ with $\omega^4=-1$ gives $(b-d)+(a+c)\omega+(b+d)\omega^2+(c-a)\omega^3$. By [F1], this product is in $2O$ exactly when all four displayed coefficients are even, which is equivalent to $a+c$ and $b+d$ even, or $a\equiv c$ and $b\equiv d\pmod2$. This proves the first criterion.

Expanding $x\bar x$ with $\bar\omega=-\omega^3$ and reducing powers gives the stated $P+\sqrt2Q$. Write $A=a+c$ and $B=b+d$ modulo $2$. Then $P\equiv A+B$ and $Q\equiv AB\pmod2$. The pair $(A+B,AB)$ is $(0,0)$ exactly for $(A,B)=(0,0)$: the other three pairs give $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$, or $(1,0)$. Since $P+\sqrt2Q$ is in $2O$ exactly when its unique power-basis coefficients are all even, equivalently when $P,Q$ are both even, the norm is in $2O$ exactly when $A=B=0$, which by step 1.1 is exactly when $\sqrt2$ divides $x$.

derivations.claim: For nonzero $z$, write its canonical form $z=a/2^r$ using [F1]. If $r>0$, then $a\bar a=2^{2r}$, so $2\mid a\bar a$ in $O$ and [F2] gives $a=\sqrt2a_1$ for some $a_1\in O$. Whenever $a_j\in O$ has $a_j\bar a_j=2^m$ with $m>0$, the same argument gives $a_j=\sqrt2a_{j+1}$ and $a_{j+1}\bar a_{j+1}=2^{m-1}$. Applying this for $m=2r,2r-1,\ldots,1$ yields $a=(\sqrt2)^{2r}a_{2r}=2^ra_{2r}$. All canonical coefficients of $a$ are then even, contradicting the minimality of $r$. Thus $r=0$ and $z\in O$.

Write $z=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3$ with integer coefficients. Direct multiplication gives $z\bar z=P+\sqrt2Q=1$, where $P=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ and $Q=a(b-d)+c(b+d)$ by [F2]. Since $1,\sqrt2$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, $P=1$ and $Q=0$. Four integer squares sum to $1$ only when exactly one coefficient is $1$ or $-1$ and the others are zero. Hence $z\in\{\pm1,\pm\omega,\pm\omega^2,\pm\omega^3\}=\{\omega^j:0\le j<8\}$.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.
A rational number is an algebraic integer if and only if it is an integer. See [[def-integral-element-and-algebraic-integer]].

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

derivations.claim: The two inequalities $|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1$, together with their complex conjugates, give $|\sigma_j(u)|\le1$ for all four embeddings $j=1,3,5,7$; these are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite by [F3]. If $k=-m<0$, the definition of $k$ gives $x=(\sqrt2)^k u=(\sqrt2)^{-m}u\in O$, so $u=(\sqrt2)^m x$. Thus $|\sigma_j(x)|\le2^{-m/2}$ for every $j$. The field norm $N_{K/\mathbb Q}(x)=\prod_{j=1,3,5,7}\sigma_j(x)$ is a nonzero rational algebraic integer, hence a nonzero integer by [F2], but its modulus is at most $2^{-2m}<1$. This contradiction proves $k\ge0$.

For $k\ge0$, set $a=(\sqrt2)^ku\in O$. Then $|\sigma_j(a)|\le2^{k/2}$ for every $j$. Fourier inversion in the power basis gives
$a_r=\frac14\sum_{j\in\{1,3,5,7\}}\sigma_j(a)\omega^{-jr}$: expanding the sum, the coefficient of $a_s$ is $\frac14\sum_{j\text{ odd}}\omega^{j(s-r)}$, which equals $1$ for $s=r$ and $0$ for distinct $r,s\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Therefore $|a_r|\le\frac14\sum_j|\sigma_j(a)|\le2^{k/2}$. Since $a_r$ is an integer, it lies in the stated finite interval.

derivations.claim: Put $s=\operatorname{sde}(z)$ and $x=(\sqrt2)^s z\in O$. Minimality of $s$ implies $\sqrt2\nmid x$, since otherwise $x=\sqrt2 y$ with $y\in O$ would make $(\sqrt2)^{s-1}z=y\in O$.

Write $x=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3$ and set $A=a+c$, $B=b+d$. By [F1], $\sqrt2\nmid x$ means $(A,B)$ is not $(0,0)$ modulo $2$. The two congruences $P\equiv A+B$ and $Q\equiv AB$ show that $P,Q$ are not both even: among the three nonzero pairs $(A,B)\in\{0,1\}^2$, the pair $(A+B,AB)$ is never $(0,0)$. For $P+\sqrt2Q$, divisibility by $(\sqrt2)^2=2$ is equivalent to both coefficients $P,Q$ being even. Hence $x\bar x$ is divisible by $\sqrt2$ at most once.

Let $m\in\{0,1\}$ be the number of factors $\sqrt2$ dividing $x\bar x$; write $x\bar x=(\sqrt2)^m y$ with $y\in O$ and $\sqrt2\nmid y$. Since $|z|^2=(x\bar x)/(\sqrt2)^{2s}$, its least denominator exponent is $2s-m$: multiplying by that power gives $y$, while any smaller exponent leaves a denominator because $\sqrt2\nmid y$. Thus $\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)=2s-m$.
The hypothesis gives $2s-m\le3$ and $m\le1$, so $2s\le4$ and $s\le2$.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

derivations.claim:
Direct $2\times2$ determinants give $\det H=-1=\omega^4$,
$\det T=\omega$, $\det T^\dagger=\omega^{-1}$, $\det S=\omega^2$,
$\det S^\dagger=\omega^{-2}$, and $\det X=\det Y=\det Z=-1=\omega^4$.
Also $\det(\omega^j I)=\omega^{2j}$. Thus every one-qubit generator has
determinant an integer power of $\omega$.

By [F2], the determinant of a finite product is the product of the
generator determinants from step 1.1. The product is again an integer power
of $\omega$, including for the empty word, whose determinant is $1$.

$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.

multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

By [F7], determinant is a homomorphism on $G$, and [F2] places its image
in the finite group $\mu_8$. Therefore its kernel
$G_1=\{W\in G:\det W=1\}$ has finite index in $G$.
Let $\pi:U(2)\to PU(2)$ be the quotient map. Then $\pi(G_1)$ has finite
index in $\pi(G)$, and [F1] makes $\pi(G)$ dense. Its closure
$\overline{\pi(G_1)}$ is consequently a closed finite-index subgroup of
$PU(2)$: the dense group $\pi(G)$ is a finite union of cosets of
$\pi(G_1)$, so its closure is the same finite union of the corresponding
closed cosets of $\overline{\pi(G_1)}$. Every projective class has an
$SU(2)$ representative: write
$\det Q=e^{i\phi}$ using [F8] and multiply $Q$ by
$\lambda=e^{-i\phi/2}$.
Every $SU(2)$ matrix has eigenvalues $e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha}$; [F4]
diagonalizes it and the path $s\mapsto S\operatorname{diag}(e^{is\alpha},
e^{-is\alpha})S^*$ joins it to $I$. Thus $SU(2)$, and hence its continuous
image $PU(2)$, is connected. The complement of a finite-index closed
subgroup is a finite union of its closed cosets, so that subgroup is also
open. Since $PU(2)$ is connected, its only nonempty clopen subgroup is
$PU(2)$ itself; hence $\overline{\pi(G_1)}=PU(2)$.

Choose $\delta>0$ and, by the density just proved, a word $W\in G_1$
and a scalar $|\lambda|=1$ with $\|W-\lambda R\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\delta$.
Write the columns of $W$ and $\lambda R$ as $w_1,w_2$ and $r_1,r_2$.
Multilinearity [F5] gives
$\det W-\det(\lambda R)=\det(w_1-\lambda r_1,w_2)
+\det(\lambda r_1,w_2-\lambda r_2)$. For $x=(x_1,x_2)^T$ and
$y=(y_1,y_2)^T$, expanding both sides gives
$|\det(x,y)|^2=\|x\|^2\|y\|^2-|\langle x,y\rangle|^2
=|x_1|^2|y_2|^2+|x_2|^2|y_1|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(x_1y_2\bar x_2\bar y_1)
\le\|x\|^2\|y\|^2$. Since the columns are unit vectors and each column
difference has norm less than $\delta$ by [F6],
$|1-\lambda^2|\le2\delta$.

Put $a=|\lambda-1|$ and $b=|\lambda+1|$. Then $a^2+b^2=4$ and
$ab=|1-\lambda^2|\le2\delta$. Since $\max(a,b)\ge\sqrt2$ from
$a^2+b^2=4$, we have $\min(a,b)=ab/\max(a,b)\le\sqrt2\,\delta$.
Choose $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ attaining this minimum. By the triangle
inequality and $\|R\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1$,
$\|W-\sigma R\|_{\mathrm{op}}< (1+\sqrt2)\delta$. The scalar $-I$ is a
word in $G$: direct multiplication gives
$$X=HZH=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad XZ=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad (XZ)^2=-I.$$
Thus $\sigma W\in G_1$, and
$\|\sigma W-R\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|W-\sigma R\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is less than
$(1+\sqrt2)\delta$. Because $\det(-I)=1$ and $\det W=1$, this scalar
correction leaves the determinant equal to $1$. Choosing
$\delta<\varepsilon/(1+\sqrt2)$ proves the claim.

$$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon,$$

permitted. The operator norm is the finite-dimensional norm from

Put $\Delta=R_z(\theta)^*U$. It is unitary and has determinant $1$, so
[F2] gives eigenvalues $e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha}$ for some
$\alpha\in[0,\pi]$. From the displayed matrices,
$\operatorname{tr}\Delta=e^{i\theta/2}u+e^{-i\theta/2}\bar u
=2\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$. Hence $\cos\alpha=
\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$.

Left multiplication by $R_z(\theta)^*$ preserves vector norms, so [F3]
gives $\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|I-\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.
Diagonalizing $\Delta$ by [F2] shows this norm is
$\max(|1-e^{i\alpha}|,|1-e^{-i\alpha}|)=2\sin(\alpha/2)$.
Therefore its square is $2-2\cos\alpha
=2-2\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$. Since both sides are nonnegative,
the norm bound is equivalent to the stated real-part inequality.

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. Let $D$ be a finite ordered quantum register and let $A$ be an ordered register of $k\ge0$ ancilla qubits, with Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_D$ and $\mathcal H_A$. Write $|0_A\rangle=|0^k\rangle$, including $|0_A\rangle=1$ when $k=0$. Let $U$ be a unitary on $\mathcal H_D\otimes\mathcal H_A$ and let $V$ be a unitary on $\mathcal H_D$.

The register $A$ is a **clean ancilla register for $U$ and $V$** when
$$
U(|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|0_A\rangle)=V|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|0_A\rangle
$$
for every vector $|\psi\rangle_D$. Thus the data operation is independent of the input vector and all clean wires return exactly to zero.

The register $A$ is a **dirty ancilla register for $U$ and $V$** when the operator identity $U=V\otimes I_A$ holds on $\mathcal H_D\otimes\mathcal H_A$. Equivalently, every product input $|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|\eta\rangle_A$ is mapped to $V|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|\eta\rangle_A$, with the same $V$ for every data and ancilla vector. This requires exact restoration of an arbitrary, initially unknown ancilla state and forbids residual data–ancilla correlation.

Let $G$ be the group of exact one-qubit Clifford+T matrix words, and let
$SU(2)=\{U\in U(2):\det U=1\}$. For every $R\in SU(2)$ and every
$\varepsilon>0$, some $W\in G$ satisfies $\det W=1$ and
$\|R-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\varepsilon$.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

Let $\theta\in\mathbb R$, $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, and
$$U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\bar t\\t&\bar u\end{pmatrix}\in SU(2).$$
Then
$$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\varepsilon^2/2.$$

By [F2,F3], the entries of $T,T^\dagger$ lie in $D$. Also
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ and $1/\sqrt2=(\omega-\omega^3)/2$, so every
entry of $H$ lies in $D$. The ring $D$ is closed under complex conjugation
because $\bar\omega=\omega^{-1}=\omega^7\in D$. Apply [F1] to
$R_z(\theta)\in SU(2)$ and choose an exact word $U$ with $\det U=1$ and
$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\varepsilon$. Every entry of $U$ lies in
$D$ because each generator has entries in $D$ and products of matrices over
a subring remain over that subring. Let the first column be
$(u,t)^T$. It is a unit vector; its orthogonal unit vector
$(-\bar t,\bar u)^T$ is therefore the second column up to a unit scalar
$\lambda$. The determinant of the resulting matrix is $\lambda$, so
$\det U=1$ forces $\lambda=1$. Hence
$U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\bar t\\t&\bar u\end{pmatrix}$ and
$t^\dagger t=1-u^\dagger u$.

Applying $\bullet$ to $U^*U=I$ preserves products and fixes $I$; [F4]
also makes it commute with the adjoint. Thus $U^\bullet$ is unitary, and its
first-column norm gives $|u^\bullet|^2+|t^\bullet|^2=1$. The original first
column similarly gives $|u|^2+|t|^2=1$, so $|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1$.

The strict approximation in step 1.1 and [F5] imply
$\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)>1-\varepsilon^2/2$, hence the required
weak inequality. Together with step 1.1 this gives a grid candidate and an
exact solution of its norm equation.

$$U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\omega^j\bar v\\v&\omega^j\bar u\end{pmatrix},\qquad |u|^2+|v|^2=1.$$

Let $(u,v)^T$ be a unit vector with entries in $D$, and put
$s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)$. If $s>3$, then some $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ has

$$\operatorname{sde}\!\left(\left|\frac{u+\omega^{-k}v}{\sqrt2}\right|^2\right)=s-1.$$

Moreover, every such unit column with $s\le3$ is prepared exactly from
$|0\rangle$ by a word in $H,T,T^\dagger$. A complete coefficient-and-word
table for the finite base set is recorded at
`research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.

derivations.claim: If $U$ is a finite Clifford+T circuit matrix, [F1] puts all its entries in $D$.

Conversely, let $U\in U(2)$ have entries in $D$. By [F2] its first column $(u,v)^T$ is a normalized column. Apply the descent in [F3] repeatedly while $s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)>3$. Each step replaces the current matrix $M$ by $HT^{-k}M$ and decreases the nonnegative integer $s$ by exactly one; hence after finitely many steps the first column lies in the base regime.

By [F3], the base column has a word $W_0$ with $W_0|0\rangle=(u_0,v_0)^T$. Reversing each descent step by prepending its recorded $T^kH$ gives a word $W$ with first column equal to the original $(u,v)^T$. The unitary $W^*U$ has first column $(1,0)^T$, so orthogonality of its columns makes it $\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ for a unit scalar $\lambda$. Its entries lie in $D$, since $W,U$ have entries in that ring. Therefore [F4] gives $\lambda=\omega^j$, and $U=WT^j$ is a finite Clifford+T word.
Both implications are proved. The proof constructs the converse word with only exact coefficient operations and the finite base lookup; no approximation, ancilla, or multi-qubit inference is used.

$$\omega^q T^a H T^{b_1}H\cdots H T^{b_{h-1}}H T^c X^e,$$

where all $b_i$ are odd, exponents are read modulo $8$, and $e\in\{0,1\}$. For $h=0$ interpret this as $\omega^qT^aX^e$. The rewriting never increases either resource count. Each odd power uses one T gate and even powers use none. A reduced word with $h\ge2$ has $\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)=h+1$; with $h=1$ the exponent is $2$, and with $h=0$ the squared entry is $0$ or $1$. Consequently reduced words minimize H count among all words for the same matrix up to global phase.

following exact procedure.

1. Test $U^*U=I$ by rational coefficient arithmetic. If it fails, return
   `INVALID`.
2. Set $M=U$ and an empty list $K$. While
   $s=\operatorname{sde}(|M_{00}|^2)>3$, test $k=0,1,2,3$ in that order and
   choose the first for which
$\operatorname{sde}(|(HT^{-k}M)_{00}|^2)=s-1$. Append $k$ to $K$ and replace
$M$ by $HT^{-k}M$.
3. Look up the first column of $M$ in the complete base-column table at
   `research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
   Let $W_0$ be its stored H/T preparation word. Compute
   $W_0^*M=\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ exactly and find $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$
   with $\lambda=\omega^j$.
4. If $K=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ in reduction order, form the exact matrix-word
factorization
$$U=(T^{k_1}H)\cdots(T^{k_r}H)W_0T^j.$$
For the chronological output, emit $T^j$ first, then the stored chronological
gate list for $W_0$, then for $i=r,r-1,\ldots,1$ emit $H$ followed by
$T^{k_i}$. The QC09 semantics put later gates on the left, so this list has the
displayed matrix product.
5. Reduce this word by the exact stack rewriting in
   [[lem-qc-hadamard-reduced-word-denominators]]: move Pauli $X$ factors to
   the right, combine diagonal powers modulo eight, and replace each
   $HT^{2r}H$ by its zero- or one-H Clifford expression until all interior
   diagonal powers are odd. Retain the scalar phase $\omega^qI$ produced by
   these identities in the exact output. Emit even powers as $S,Z$ factors
   and odd powers as one $T$ or $T^\dagger$ with free $S,Z$ factors, then
   return the reduced factors in reverse order as the chronological list.

table uses exact rational coefficients; no numerical equality tolerance is

Let $\bullet$ be the automorphism of $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$ defined in
[[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], so $\omega^\bullet=-\omega=\omega^5$,
and let $u\in D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|u|\le1$ and $|u^\bullet|\le1$. Then $k=\operatorname{sde}(u)\ge0$. If
$a=(\sqrt2)^ku=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$, then

Thus for each fixed $k$ only finitely many coefficient vectors can occur; the

derivations.claim: By [F2,F3], before the final reduction the compiler has an exact word for $U$. By [F1] its final reduced word is exact and H-optimal, and $n\ge4$ makes its H count $h=n-1$. Write its endpoint exponents $a,c$ and its trailing Pauli factor $X^e$ as in [F1]. Each of the $h-1$ odd interior powers costs one T, so its T count is $h-1+p(a)+p(c)$, where $p(r)=r\bmod2\in\{0,1\}$.

Every Clifford block generated by $H,S,X,Y,Z$ reduces by [F1] to at most one H: all diagonal exponents remain even during that reduction. Splitting any word containing $t$ T gates into $t+1$ Clifford blocks therefore proves $h(V)\le t(V)+1$ for every represented $V$. This argument applies to $T^\dagger$ equally.

Choose $\ell$ and $j$ with $a+\ell$ and $c-j$ odd. Then $HT^\ell UT^jH$ has an odd-interior reduced word with $h+2$ H gates: commute $X^e$ past $T^jH$ using the identities in [F1], which changes only the sign of $j$ and adds a free terminal $Z$ when $e=1$. Its H count is therefore minimal. Conversely if either parity condition fails, the adjacent even-interior pair reduces, giving strictly fewer than $h+2$ H gates. Thus the extension condition is equivalent to $p(\ell)=1-p(a)$ and $p(j)=1-p(c)$.

Apply step 1.2 to the extended matrix $V=HT^\ell UT^jH$. Multiplication by these endpoint factors gives $t(V)\le t(U)+p(\ell)+p(j)$, while $h(V)=h+2$ gives $t(V)\ge h+1$. Consequently $t(U)\ge h+1-p(\ell)-p(j)=h-1+p(a)+p(c)$. Step 1.1 attains this bound, proving simultaneous optimality and both formulas. The same argument proves the endpoint formula for every reduced word with at least one H, since its extension still has at least three H gates and [F1] applies.

There are $n-3$ descent iterations and a constant-size base lookup. Each trial uses boundedly many coefficient additions, sign permutations, multiplications by fixed ring constants, and denominator tests. At every iteration all embeddings of the current unitary remain unitary, so all embedded entries have modulus at most one. For a positive squared-entry exponent, the complementary squared norm has the same exponent: subtracting its primitive numerator from the positive power of $\sqrt2$ leaves it primitive. Thus [F5] bounds every entry exponent by $(n+1)/2$; the base regime is bounded by [F3]. By [F4] all numerator coefficients have $O(n+1)$ bits. Denominator tests need no integer multiplication: for $x=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3\ne0$, let $m$ be the minimum of the binary trailing-zero counts of its nonzero coefficients, and put $y=x/2^m$. Its $\sqrt2$-valuation is $2m+\delta$, where $\delta=1$ exactly when both opposite-coefficient sums of $y$ are even. Indeed $y$ is not divisible by $2$, so it can contain at most one factor $\sqrt2$. For the resulting primitive numerator $z$, its norm has zero or one factor $\sqrt2$ by [F5]; this factor occurs exactly when $\sum z_i$ is even, since the rational coefficient of $z\bar z$ is $\sum z_i^2$. These parity and trailing-zero scans take $O(n+1)$ bit operations. Every descent trial therefore costs $O(n+1)$ bits and boundedly many ring operations, with coefficient valuations counted as linear binary scans.

The initial word has $O(n+1)$ gates and its stack reduction is linear by [F1], retaining only exponents modulo eight and a scalar exponent modulo eight. The preceding bounds give $O(n+1)$ ring operations and $O((n+1)^2)$ bit operations overall. Any word's total H/T count is at least $h(U)=n-1$; the output has $h+t\le2h+1=O(n+1)$ by step 1.1. Hence $n+1=\Theta(n_{\rm opt}+1)$, proving the claimed bounds.

Input exact reals $\theta$, $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, an exact-real comparison
capability for the grid inequalities, and either an integer-factorization
oracle or bounded mode with a declared additional factor-attempt budget
$Q(k)\ge0$ (default zero); a fixed finite budget is allowed. No bit encoding for
arbitrary reals is implicit. Use an independent random stream for the grid
iterator and fresh independent streams for each randomized norm call; the
candidate order depends only on the grid stream, not on norm-call outcomes.

1. Enumerate $u$ from
   [[alg-qc-cyclotomic-scaled-grid-and-norm-solver]] in increasing denominator
   exponent. For each candidate, compute $\xi=1-|u|^2$. In oracle mode
   obtain the complete integer factorization and invoke the efficient exact
   norm subprocedure; the finite-search complete solver is an alternative.
   In bounded mode use the calibrated capped prime attempt and its optional
   budgeted extra factoring attempt, accepting only an exact certificate.
2. If it returns `FACTOR_TIMEOUT` or `NO_SOLUTION`, continue to the next
   candidate. For each returned $t$ with $t^*t=\xi$, form
   $U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\bar t\\t&\bar u\end{pmatrix}$ and
   $U'=TUT^\dagger$.
3. Run [[alg-qc-exact-single-qubit-clifford-t-synthesis]] on both matrices.
   Return the word with smaller exact T-count; break ties by lexicographic
   gate word. If a finite total candidate budget is supplied and is exhausted
   first, return `TIMEOUT`.

The exact grid-to-error equivalence is proved in
[[lem-qc-rz-epsilon-region-equivalence]]. The unbounded factoring-oracle mode
uses the complete efficient solver from the norm procedure, or the finite
alternative [[thm-qc-cyclotomic-norm-equation-decision]]. Successful
termination (almost surely for the randomized efficient mode) under the stated
terminating exact-real comparisons is proved in
[[thm-qc-rz-approximation-correct-on-termination]]. A finite-budget call can
return `TIMEOUT`. The complete finite-search norm mode gives no polynomial
arithmetic-time guarantee.

Let $\theta\in\mathbb R$, $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, and
$$U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\bar t\\t&\bar u\end{pmatrix}\in SU(2).$$
Then
$$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\varepsilon^2/2.$$

For $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, there are $u,t\in D$
such that
$$|u|\le1,\qquad |u^\bullet|\le1,\qquad \operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\varepsilon^2/2,\qquad t^\dagger t=1-u^\dagger u.$$
Thus the scaled grid has at least one candidate whose norm equation is
solvable.

Let $\bullet$ be the automorphism of $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$ defined in
[[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], so $\omega^\bullet=-\omega=\omega^5$,
and let $u\in D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|u|\le1$ and $|u^\bullet|\le1$. Then $k=\operatorname{sde}(u)\ge0$. If
$a=(\sqrt2)^ku=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$, then

$$|a_j|\le2^{k/2}\quad(0\le j\le3).$$

Thus for each fixed $k$ only finitely many coefficient vectors can occur; the
integer search may be restricted to
$|a_j|\le\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$.

For every unitary $U\in M_2(D)$, the procedure in
[[alg-qc-exact-single-qubit-clifford-t-synthesis]] terminates and returns a
finite one-qubit Clifford+T word whose exact matrix is $U$.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For every $\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]$ there is a terminating exact
algorithm deciding whether $t^\dagger t=\xi$ has a solution
$t\in D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$, and returning such a solution when one
exists. A supplied prime factorization of the numerator of
$\xi^\bullet\xi$ is permissible but unnecessary for the finite-search
version below. No polynomial runtime bound is asserted.

More explicitly, reject a negative real embedding; handle $\xi=0$ by
$t=0$. Otherwise choose $r\ge0$ with $\eta=4^r\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$
and factor $\eta$ into primes of $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$. Group the prime
associate classes into orbits of complex conjugation. There is a solution
exactly when every conjugation-fixed class has even exponent. The
conjugation-paired classes have equal exponents automatically. Allocate half
of each fixed exponent, and the whole exponent to one representative of each
pair, to form $s$. Recover a real unit $v$ with
$v^2=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$; then $t=vs/2^r$ is an exact solution.

The iterator [[alg-qc-rz-efficient-scaled-grid-iterator]] enumerates exactly once every $u\in\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$ satisfying $u\in A$, $u^\bullet\in B$, in increasing least $\sqrt2$ denominator exponent. Let $L=1+\log(1/\varepsilon)$. Its startup costs $O(L^2)$ ideal exact-real arithmetic/comparison operations. In a layer $k$ having $N$ solutions, its explicit proposal domain has size $M\le C(N+1)$ for an absolute constant $C$, without filtering already emitted lower-denominator points. Empty layers cost $\operatorname{poly}(k+L)$. For $1\le j\le N$, the expected work through its first $j$ distinct outputs is $O(j(1+\log j)\operatorname{poly}(k+L))$; the $r$th moment of that prefix work is $O_r(j^{2r}\operatorname{poly}(k+L)^r)$ for every fixed positive integer $r$. Complete-layer work is $O((N+1)\operatorname{poly}(k+L))$ in expectation. These are arithmetic bounds with random-bit generation charged, and do not assert bit-time bounds for unspecified real inputs or worst-case polynomial delay.

Put $R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and $D=O[1/2]$, with $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. Given $\xi\in R[1/2]$ and a valid complete rational-prime factorization of the nonzero numerator $n$ in the reduced fraction $\xi^\bullet\xi=n/2^\ell$, there is an exact randomized algorithm returning $t\in D$ with $t^\dagger t=\xi$, or correctly reporting that no such $t$ exists. Zero input requires no factorization. The algorithm terminates almost surely and has expected bit cost polynomial in the total binary length $L$ of the explicitly encoded rational coefficients of $\xi$ and the supplied factorization. Denominators are ordinary binary integers, not compressed exponent encodings. The algorithm does not compute or verify rational primality of the promised prime factors.

In particular, suppose $0\le\xi,\xi^\bullet\le1$, and $k$ is the least nonnegative integer with $(\sqrt2)^k\xi\in R$. Given the factorization of $n$, the expected cost, including exact solution recovery or a correct negative answer, is polynomial in $k+1$ when $\xi$ is supplied in reduced coefficient form. For a grid candidate $u\in D$ with least $\sqrt2$-denominator exponent $h$, its residual $\xi=1-u^\dagger u$ has least exponent at most $2h$. Under the same embedding bounds, $n\le4^h$ and the residual solver has expected cost polynomial in $h+1$. The unrestricted cost includes the bit length of the coefficients, rather than depending on $\log n$ alone.

For the stated grid residual with $n$ prime, or $n\in\{0,1\}$, a concrete schoolbook implementation of this algorithm has expected bit cost at most $P(h)=2^{200}(h+1)^{20}$. This explicit bound includes input reading in reduced coefficient form and exact verification of a returned solution. Bit cost counts Boolean operations and bit reads/writes on binary arrays; multi-bit arithmetic is performed by the schoolbook loops detailed below. It gives a numerical cap for interrupted attempts; it makes no correctness or termination assertion about calling prime-specific branches with a composite integer falsely presented as prime.

If the procedure returns, its successful candidate satisfies the
scaled-grid real-part inequality by construction and [A2] gives the exact
norm equation. Thus $|u|^2+|t|^2=1$; multiplying the displayed
matrix by its conjugate transpose gives $U^*U=I$ and
$\det U=|u|^2+|t|^2=1$. Therefore $U$ is in the form required by [F2], which
gives
$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon$.

Since $T$ and $R_z(\theta)$ are diagonal, they commute. By [F7],
unitary left and right multiplication preserve the operator norm: the
left factor preserves every vector norm, and the right factor bijects the
unit sphere to itself. Thus
$\|R_z(\theta)-TUT^\dagger\|_{\mathrm{op}}
=\|T^\dagger R_z(\theta)T-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}
=\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Thus both compiler inputs meet the same
error bound.

The exact compiler conclusion [F5] makes each returned word's matrix
equal its selected input. Since the procedure chooses between $U$ and
$U'$, step 1.2 proves the returned word satisfies the required bound.

By [F3] there is a solvable grid candidate with some finite exponent $k$.
By [F4], each layer from $0$ through $k$ has finitely many coefficient
vectors. The finite-search alternative checks them all; the default iterator
enumerates precisely the candidates and finishes each preceding layer by [F9].
By [F8], each norm call terminates and it succeeds when that candidate is
reached; the finitely many comparison and oracle calls terminate by [A1]. Therefore
the unbounded loop terminates after finitely many earlier layers and
candidates. A bounded call may stop with TIMEOUT before this point.

For efficient factored mode, take a fixed exponent $k$ for one solvable
candidate from [F3]. There are only finitely many candidates in layers
through $k$, independent of their within-layer order. The iterator finishes
each preceding layer for every random-bit sequence by [F9]. On each of these
finitely many algebraic inputs, the norm call terminates with probability
one by [F10]. With fresh independent solver bits this remains true
conditional on the history, so the finite union of nontermination events
has probability zero. On its complement the same candidate argument as in
step 2.1 gives successful return.

$\varepsilon$. For every fixed nonnegative integer $d$,

the stream is ordered by exponent and the solver is complete, its exponent
$k$ is the least exponent of any solvable candidate. By [F3], taking the
smaller compiled count returns $f(k)$, the minimum across determinant-one
feasible classes, because $f$ is nondecreasing. By [F2] this is the global
minimum. For $\varepsilon\ge c_0$, the zero-T Clifford has an upper-left
root of unity and occurs in layer zero, so this reasoning still returns
zero.

For the bounded-factorization branch let $J$ be the index of the first
guaranteed success event described below. Use [F11] to combine each modelled prime event with its independently
successful capped call. Conditional on the iterator order these events are
independent with probability at least $c/(2(k_j+1))$. The procedure succeeds
no later than their first index $J$; immediate success at $n=0$ or $1$ can
only improve this bound.
By [F7], $J$ is finite almost surely,
$\mathbb E[J]=O(L)$, and
$\mathbb E[\log_2J]=O(1+\log L)$. If $\varepsilon\ge c_0$, layer zero
already returns a Clifford under [A2], so its count and the number of
lower-count solutions are zero. Hence suppose $\varepsilon<c_0$.

By [F3], the returned count satisfies $m\le f(k_J)$.
Every feasible class of count below $m$ therefore has exponent strictly
below $k_J$, since its class minimum is $f(k)$ and $f$ is nondecreasing.
By [F2] these classes cover all feasible solutions. Distinct classes have
distinct candidates and occur before index $J$, so their number is at most
$J-1$. Taking expectations proves the lower-count solution bound.

Choose the best and second-best feasible classes, breaking equal-count
ties by increasing exponent, and let their exponents be $k'$ and $k''$.
Since their class counts are $f(k)$ and $f$ is nondecreasing, this choice
has $k'\le k''$. The two classes are distinct candidates, so $k_2\le k''$.
By [F3,F4],
$m\le2k_J\le2k''+4\lceil\log_2J\rceil
\le m''+2+4\lceil\log_2J\rceil
\le m''+6+4\log_2J$.
Taking expectations and applying step 2.1 gives
$\mathbb E[m]\le m''+O(1+\log L)$, which is the stated asymptotic bound.
The existence of two feasible classes is included in the solvability
interface: [A1,F6] give almost surely infinitely many solvable successes,
since the tail product after every finite index tends to zero by [F7].

Write $C_j$ for the iterator work through its $j$th global candidate,
with no norm calls interleaved. The exponent sequence $k_j$ depends only on
the number of distinct candidates in each layer, so it is unchanged by the
iterator's randomized tie order. By [F4,F8], for some fixed $D$,
$\sqrt{\mathbb E[C_j^2]}\le C(j+1)^2(L+1+\log(j+1))^D$.
The stopping tail from [F7] holds uniformly conditional on every complete
iterator order, hence also unconditionally:
$\Pr(J>j)\le\exp(-j/(a+b\ln j))$, with $a=O(L)$ and fixed $b>0$.

expectation of $(X/\sqrt{\mathbb E[X^2]}-Z/\sqrt{\mathbb E[Z^2]})^2$

vanishes its term is zero. This sum is polynomial in $L$. Indeed, for $j\ge a$ the tail proof of [F7]

derivations.claim:
For $x=a+b\sqrt2\in\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ put
$N_R(x)=|a^2-2b^2|$. For $z=A+B\omega$ with $A,B\in\mathbb Q(i)$ put
$N_O(z)=|A^2-iB^2|^2=|z|^2|z^\bullet|^2$.
These functions are multiplicative, positive on nonzero elements, and take
positive integer values on nonzero elements of their respective rings:
$A,B\in\mathbb Z[i]$ for $z\in O$, and
$z z^\bullet=A^2-iB^2\in\mathbb Z[i]$. Integer norm one is equivalent to
being a unit: the converse follows by multiplicativity, and the forward
implication follows by taking the product of the other conjugates divided by
the norm (with a sign in $R$). All coordinates of that inverse remain in the
ring.

To divide in $R$, round the rational coefficients of a quotient to nearest
integers. Its error $e=a+b\sqrt2$ has $|a|,|b|\le1/2$, so
$N_R(e)=|a^2-2b^2|\le1/2<1$. To divide in $O$, express a quotient as
$A+B\omega$ and round $A,B$ to Gaussian integers. For the errors $C,D$,
$|C|^2,|D|^2\le1/2$, whence
$N_O(C+D\omega)=|C^2-iD^2|^2\le(|C|^2+|D|^2)^2\le1$.
If the last upper bound equals one, all four real coordinates of $C,D$
are $\pm1/2$. Then $C^2,D^2$ are purely imaginary of magnitude $1/2$,
so $C^2$ and $-iD^2$ are perpendicular and the actual norm is $1/2$.
Otherwise the displayed bound is already strict. Multiplicativity therefore
gives a remainder of norm strictly below that of the divisor in both rings.
This proves the Euclidean assertions, including ties in rounding.

Repeated division terminates because nonzero remainder norms strictly
decrease through positive integers. Back substitution expresses the gcd as a
linear combination. If an irreducible $p$ does not divide $a$, the gcd of
$p,a$ is a unit, so multiplying a Bezout identity by $b$ shows that
$p\mid ab$ implies $p\mid b$. Thus irreducibles are prime. A nonunit
has a factorization into irreducibles by induction on its norm: a proper
factorization has two factors of norm at least two, each of smaller norm.
The prime-divisor property and cancellation give uniqueness up to ordering
and units. Divisibility is decidable by computing the quotient in the field
and checking its integral coordinates; two elements are associates exactly
when their quotient has integral coordinates and norm one.

The real elements of $O$ are exactly $R$. Indeed, for
$z=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2 i+a_3\omega^3$, its imaginary part is
$a_2+(a_1+a_3)/\sqrt2$; irrationality of $\sqrt2$ makes this zero exactly
when $a_2=0$ and $a_3=-a_1$. The real part is then
$a_0+a_1\sqrt2$. A real unit of $O$ consequently is a unit of $R$, since
its inverse is real too. Also $\lambda^{-1}=\sqrt2-1\in R$ and
$\lambda^\bullet=-\lambda^{-1}$.

If $u\in R$ is a unit, choose a sign and an integer power of $\lambda$
to make $v=\pm\lambda^j u$ lie in $[1,\lambda)$. Such a power exists
because $\lambda>1$. Write $v=a+b\sqrt2$. Its signed field norm is
$\pm1$, so $v^\bullet=\pm1/v$. For norm $+1$,
$a=(v+1/v)/2\in[1,\sqrt2)$, hence $a=1$; the equation
$a^2-2b^2=1$ forces $b=0$ and $v=1$. For norm $-1$,
$a=(v-1/v)/2\in[0,1)$, hence $a=0$, incompatible with
$-2b^2=-1$. This proves $u=\pm\lambda^m$. Its two embeddings are
positive exactly when the sign is positive and $m$ is even. In this case
$\lambda^{m/2}$ is the required real unit square root. Enumerating integer
powers until the exact coefficients agree recovers $m$ in finite time.
Signs and comparisons of $a+b\sqrt2$ are decided by signs of the rational
coefficients and, when necessary, comparing $a^2$ and $2b^2$.

Here is an explicit finite factor search, which makes the existence proof
algorithmic without a primality oracle for $O$. For a nonunit
$\alpha\in O$ put $M=N_O(\alpha)\ge2$ and enumerate all power-basis
integer tuples with coefficients between $-(M+3)$ and $M+3$. Test whether
such an element $d$ divides $\alpha$ and $1<N_O(d)<M$; any successful
$d$ splits $\alpha$ into smaller-norm factors. If $\alpha$ is reducible,
choose a nonunit proper divisor and multiply it by a power of the unit
$\lambda$ so $1\le|d|<\lambda$. Its norm is unchanged and less than
$M$, and $|d^\bullet|=\sqrt{N_O(d)}/|d|\le\sqrt M$.
Recovering power-basis coefficients from the two complex embeddings gives
$|a_0|,|a_2|\le(|d|+|d^\bullet|)/2$ and
$|a_1|,|a_3|\le(|d|+|d^\bullet|)/\sqrt2$.
They are all below $\lambda+\sqrt M<M+3$, so the list contains this
normalized proper divisor. Failure of the finite search therefore certifies
irreducibility. Recursing on successful factors terminates by strict norm
descent, and the residual norm-one elements supply the unit.

$(t^\dagger t)^\bullet=|t^\bullet|^2$ are nonnegative. If either real
embedding of $\xi$ is negative, reject. The signs are decidable by rational
arithmetic and squaring the rational coefficients of $a+b\sqrt2$ after
checking their signs. If either embedding is zero, injectivity of that
embedding implies $\xi=0$, and the output $t=0$ suffices. Thus the remaining
case has both embeddings strictly positive. Choose $r$ by clearing the
powers of two in the two coefficients of $\xi$; multiplication by the
positive rational square $4^r$ preserves their signs.

Put $\delta=1+\omega$ and $\lambda=1+\sqrt2$. Direct multiplication
gives $N_O(\delta)=2$, $\delta^\dagger=\omega^{-1}\delta$, and
$\delta^4=2i\lambda^2$. Norm two makes $\delta$ irreducible, hence prime
by [F1]. As $i$ and $\lambda$ are units, the last identity shows that
$2$ has just the prime associate class of $\delta$, with multiplicity
four. Every element $w\in D$ has a unique-factorization valuation
$v_\pi(w)\in\mathbb Z$ at each prime associate class of $O$, obtained
from its integral numerator minus the valuations of its power-of-two
denominator; only $v_\delta(w)$ can be negative.
Conjugation acts on these valuations by permuting the prime classes, since
it is a ring automorphism. In particular, for a fixed class,
$v_\pi(w^\dagger w)=2v_\pi(w)$.

If $w^\dagger w=\eta\in O$ for $w\in D$, then
$2v_\delta(w)=v_\delta(\eta)\ge0$, so all valuations of $w$ are
nonnegative and $w\in O$. To see the last implication without any
assumption on units of $D$, write $w=a/2^m$ with $a\in O$; its only
possible denominator class is $\delta$, and the valuation inequality says
$\delta^{4m}\mid a$, hence $2^m\mid a$. Consequently a solution to
$t^\dagger t=\xi$ gives an integral solution $w=2^r t$ to
$w^\dagger w=\eta$. Every conjugation-fixed prime exponent of $\eta$
must therefore be even. Conversely an integral solution for $\eta$ gives
a solution for $\xi$ by division by $2^r$. This proves both necessity of
the parity test and completeness of the denominator-clearing reduction.

Factor nonzero $\eta$ by the finite algorithm of [F1]. Determine
conjugation orbits by conjugating each factor and testing associates;
$\eta^\dagger=\eta$ and uniqueness of prime factorization imply that
both classes in every two-element orbit occur with the same exponent.
This is also an effective prime splitting test: each factor is assigned
either to a fixed class or to a pair of distinct conjugate classes; no
unproved classification by rational primes modulo eight is required.
If a fixed exponent is odd, reject as justified in step 1.3. Otherwise,
for each fixed class of exponent $2h$ choose its displayed prime to
power $h$, and for each pair of exponent $m$ choose one displayed prime
to power $m$. Let $s$ be the product of these choices, with empty product
one. Then $s^\dagger s$ and $\eta$ have exactly the same prime-class
exponents.

Their quotient $e=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$ is a unit of $O$ by unique
factorization, and is real. Its inverse is real too, so it is a unit of
$R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ by [F1]. Both embeddings of $s^\dagger s$ are
strictly positive, as are those of $\eta$, so both embeddings of $e$
are positive. The unit-square construction of [F1] therefore returns
$v\in R$ with $v^2=e$. Because $v^\dagger=v$,
$(vs)^\dagger(vs)=e s^\dagger s=\eta$, and division by $2^r$ gives
the claimed $t$. All loops terminate: denominator clearing is finite,
factorization terminates, associate tests are exact, the factor list is
finite, and square-root recovery terminates for a positive real unit.
Together with the rejection cases and necessity this proves the entire
decision and construction claim.

When $h=1$, every entry has modulus $1/\sqrt2$, and [F4] gives exponent $1$ for every entry; thus $k=1$.

Together with step 1.1, every case with $h\ge1$ has $h\in\{2k-2,2k-1\}$, except that $h=0$ was treated separately.

For every integer $a$ and odd prime $p$,

$$\left(\frac ap\right)\equiv a^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.$$

For an odd prime $p$, exactly $(p-1)/2$ nonzero classes are quadratic residues modulo $p$, and exactly $(p-1)/2$ are quadratic nonresidues. Each nonzero quadratic residue has exactly two square roots modulo $p$, while each nonresidue has none.

For every prime $p$, the operations of addition and multiplication on
$\mathbb Z/p$ make it a field ([[def-field]]).

derivations.claim: Reduce $a$ modulo $p$. If $p=2$, return its residue; if $a=0$, return zero. Otherwise [F1] rejects exactly the nonsquares by testing $a^{(p-1)/2}=-1$. In the remaining case write $p-1=2^s q$ with $q$ odd and $s\ge1$. Repeatedly sample $z$ uniformly from $1,\ldots,p-1$ until $z^{(p-1)/2}=-1$. Uniform sampling is implemented by drawing $\lceil\log_2p\rceil$ bits and rejecting zero and integers at least $p$. Each draw is accepted with probability at least $1/4$, and each accepted $z$ is a nonsquare with probability $1/2$ by [F2]; thus this search has bounded expected trials and terminates almost surely.

Set $x=a^{(q+1)/2}$, $t=a^q$, $c=z^q$ and $M=s$, all modulo $p$. Then $x^2=at$, $c$ has exact multiplicative order $2^M$, and $t^{2^{M-1}}=1$ by the tests in step 1.1. While $t\ne1$, find the least $m\ge1$ with $t^{2^m}=1$ by successive squaring; it satisfies $m<M$. Put $b=c^{2^{M-m-1}}$ and replace $(x,t,c,M)$ by $(xb,tb^2,b^2,m)$. The identity $x^2=at$ is preserved. The old $t$ has order exactly $2^m$, so $t^{2^{m-1}}=-1$: in a field, the only roots of $X^2-1$ are $1,-1$ by factorization. Likewise $b^2$ has order $2^m$ and its $2^{m-1}$-st power is $-1$. Therefore the new $t$ has order dividing $2^{m-1}$, while the new $c$ has order $2^m$. The invariants are maintained and $M$ strictly decreases. After at most $s$ iterations, $t=1$ and $x^2=a$. Return $x$.

Put $B=1+\lceil\log_2p\rceil$. Every modular integer has $O(B)$ bits. Schoolbook multiplication and division use $O(B^2)$ bit operations; binary repeated squaring computes a power with $O(B)$-bit exponent in $O(B)$ modular multiplications. These bounds follow directly by forming at most $B$ shifted rows for multiplication and eliminating at most $B$ quotient digits for division. Step 1.1 uses an expected bounded number of such powers. Each of the at most $B$ iterations in step 1.2 uses at most $O(B)$ modular multiplications to find $m$ and compute $b$. Its total cost is $O(B^4)$. Initial reduction has cost polynomial in the original length of $a$ and $p$. Thus the algorithm has the asserted expected bit bound; only the nonsquare search is randomized, and its outcome never changes the correctness of the final answer.

Put $R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$\lambda=1+\sqrt2$. Both rings are norm-Euclidean domains and hence unique
factorization domains with effective gcd and associate tests. There is a
terminating finite-search algorithm factoring every nonzero element of $O$
into primes and a unit. The units of $R$ are exactly $\pm\lambda^j$
($j\in\mathbb Z$); a unit is positive at both real embeddings if and only
if it is a square of a unit of $R$. These assertions include effective square
root recovery. No polynomial runtime bound is asserted for finite-search
factorization.

For every $\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]$ there is a terminating exact
algorithm deciding whether $t^\dagger t=\xi$ has a solution
$t\in D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$, and returning such a solution when one
exists. A supplied prime factorization of the numerator of
$\xi^\bullet\xi$ is permissible but unnecessary for the finite-search
version below. No polynomial runtime bound is asserted.

More explicitly, reject a negative real embedding; handle $\xi=0$ by
$t=0$. Otherwise choose $r\ge0$ with $\eta=4^r\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$
and factor $\eta$ into primes of $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$. Group the prime
associate classes into orbits of complex conjugation. There is a solution
exactly when every conjugation-fixed class has even exponent. The
conjugation-paired classes have equal exponents automatically. Allocate half
of each fixed exponent, and the whole exponent to one representative of each
pair, to form $s$. Recover a real unit $v$ with
$v^2=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$; then $t=vs/2^r$ is an exact solution.

Given a prime integer $p$ and an integer $a$, there is an exact randomized algorithm that returns a square root of $a$ modulo $p$ or correctly reports that none exists. With ordinary binary integers, schoolbook arithmetic and independent unbiased random bits, its expected bit cost is polynomial in the input length; after reducing $a$ modulo $p$, it is $O((1+\log p)^4)$. Every returned answer is correct, and the algorithm terminates with probability one. The input promise that $p$ is prime is not a primality test.

For every odd prime $p$,

$$\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}.$$

Equivalently, $(-1/p)=1$ if and only if $p\equiv1\pmod4$, while $(-1/p)=-1$ if and only if $p\equiv3\pmod4$.

For every odd prime $p$,

$$\left(\frac2p\right)=(-1)^{(p^2-1)/8}.$$

Equivalently, $(2/p)=1$ if and only if $p\equiv1$ or $7\pmod8$, while $(2/p)=-1$ if and only if $p\equiv3$ or $5\pmod8$.

For every odd prime $p$ and all integers $a,b$,

$$\left(\frac{ab}{p}\right)=\left(\frac ap\right)\left(\frac bp\right).$$

Consequently, if $p\nmid c$, then $(ac^2/p)=(a/p)$.

For every prime $p$, the operations of addition and multiplication on
$\mathbb Z/p$ make it a field ([[def-field]]).

derivations.claim: Reject if either real embedding of $\xi$ is negative, and return zero if $\xi=0$. Signs of $a+b\sqrt2$ are determined by coefficient signs and comparison of $a^2$ with $2b^2$, so these are exact polynomial bit operations. A zero real embedding implies $\xi=0$ by injectivity. Otherwise both embeddings are positive. Clear a rational square denominator by choosing the least $r\ge0$ with $\eta=4^r\xi\in R$. Since the input uses explicit denominators, $r=O(L)$ and $\eta$ has $O(L)$-bit coefficients. Its positive rational norm is $N_R(\eta)=2^{4r-\ell}n$, so its factorization is obtained from the supplied one by adjoining the known factor $2$. All its prime factors and their multiplicities have total size polynomial in $L$.

Here are polynomial bit gcd and associate procedures for [F1], with coefficient growth controlled. Use $N_R(a+b\sqrt2)=|a^2-2b^2|$ and $N_O(z)=|z|^2|z^\bullet|^2$. The real coefficient-rounding error has norm at most $1/2$. Write the cyclotomic rounding error as $C+D\omega$, where $C=x+iy$, $D=z+it$ and $|x|,|y|,|z|,|t|\le1/2$. Put $S=|C|^2+|D|^2$. If $S\le9/10$, then $N_O(C+D\omega)=|C^2-iD^2|^2\le S^2\le81/100$. If $S>9/10$, each of the four squared real coordinates exceeds $3/20$, since the other three sum to at most $3/4$. Thus $|\operatorname{Re}C^2|,|\operatorname{Re}D^2|<1/10$ and $|\operatorname{Im}C^2|,|\operatorname{Im}D^2|\le1/2$. Expanding the square gives $|C^2-iD^2|^2\le |C|^4+|D|^4+2(|\operatorname{Re}C^2||\operatorname{Im}D^2|+|\operatorname{Im}C^2||\operatorname{Re}D^2|)\le1/2+1/5=7/10$. Hence every cyclotomic remainder contracts the norm by at most $\rho=81/100$. As $(81/100)^4<1/2$, every four nonzero divisions halve the norm. This explicit estimate needs no compactness premise.

Before and after each division, balance any nonzero remainder $z$ by multiplying it by a power of $\lambda$, which changes neither its norm nor the generated principal ideal. In $R$ arrange $\sqrt{N_R(z)}\le|z|<\lambda\sqrt{N_R(z)}$; in $O$ arrange $N_O(z)^{1/4}\le|z|<\lambda N_O(z)^{1/4}$. The other embedding then has comparable magnitude, since their absolute product is respectively $N_R(z)$ or $\sqrt{N_O(z)}$. The fixed inverse linear conversion from embeddings to power-basis coordinates bounds every balanced coefficient by a constant times $N_R(z)^{1/2}$ or $N_O(z)^{1/4}$. All comparisons can be performed without numerical approximations by squaring and comparing elements of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$. For inputs with $B$-bit coordinates, the initial norm has $O(B)$ bits, and its nonzero conjugates are bounded above by $2^{O(B)}$ and below by $2^{-O(B)}$ using their integer product. Hence initial balancing uses $O(B)$ unit multiplications. Thereafter all balanced coordinates and each exact quotient have $O(B)$ bits; division in the fixed-degree number field uses a fixed number of rational operations. Rounding produces $O(B)$-bit remainders, whose balancing again uses $O(B)$ multiplications. Step 1.2 bounds the number of divisions by $O(B)$. This proves polynomial bit cost for gcds; exact quotient and associate tests have polynomial cost as well. Units used in balancing do not affect any gcd ideal.

Recover all $R$-prime classes above each odd rational prime $p$ in step 1.1 as follows. If $p\equiv3,5\pmod8$, the polynomial $X^2-2$ has no root by [F3], so $R/(p)=\mathbb F_p[X]/(X^2-2)$ is a field by [F4], and $p$ is already prime in $R$. If $p\equiv1,7\pmod8$, compute $b^2=2\pmod p$ using [F3]. Evaluation at the two distinct roots $b,-b$ identifies $R/(p)$ with $\mathbb F_p\times\mathbb F_p$: interpolation of a linear polynomial gives the inverse, since $2b$ is invertible. The gcds $\pi_+=\gcd_R(p,\sqrt2-b)$ and $\pi_-=\gcd_R(p,\sqrt2+b)$ generate the preimages of the two component kernels. Their quotients are fields, so these gcds are nonassociate primes, and the component description shows $(\pi_+\pi_-)=(p)$. These procedures give every $R$-prime over $p$ and use the modular-root algorithm and polynomial gcds of step 1.3.

For an odd $p$ and an $R$-prime $\pi$ just obtained, put $E=R/(\pi)$. Because $2$ is invertible modulo $\pi$ and $\omega=(\sqrt2/2)(1+i)$, there is an explicit isomorphism $O/(\pi)=E[i]=E[T]/(T^2+1)$: the displayed formula expresses $\omega$ in the right-hand ring, and $i=\omega^2$ expresses its inverse map. If $p\equiv7\pmod8$, then $E=\mathbb F_p$ and $T^2+1$ is irreducible by [F3]. Thus $O/(\pi)$ is a field, and $\pi$ is prime also in $O$; its class is fixed by conjugation because $\pi$ is real. If $p\equiv1,5\pmod8$, compute $b^2=-1\pmod p$ and put $h=b+i$. If $p\equiv3\pmod8$, compute $b^2=-2\pmod p$ and put $h=b+i\sqrt2$; the root exists since both characters of $-1$ and $2$ are $-1$ by [F3]. In these cases $T^2+1$ splits into distinct roots in $E$: they are $\pm b$ in the first case and $\pm b/\sqrt2$ in the second. Hence $O/(\pi)$ is a product of two fields, by the same explicit interpolation as in step 2.1. The ideals generated by $(\pi,h)$ and $(\pi,h^\dagger)$ select the two distinct component kernels. Consequently $t=\gcd_O(\pi,h)$ and $t^\dagger$ are nonassociate primes, with $\pi\sim t^\dagger t$. This proves prime recovery and its completeness, rather than merely asserting a splitting table.

Include $\delta$ as the sole prime class over $2$ by [F2]. Steps 2.1-2.2 now give a finite list of all $O$-prime classes over the rational prime divisors of $N_R(\eta)$. Every prime of $O$ dividing $\eta$ appears: it divides the integer $\eta\eta^\bullet$, and the prime-divisor property of [F1] makes it divide one of those rational primes. Repeated exact division of $\eta$ by the displayed generators, with associate tests to remove duplicate classes, therefore gives its full prime-class exponent list. The remaining quotient has norm one and is a unit, since otherwise unique factorization would supply a missing prime divisor. Compute conjugation orbits by conjugating the generators and testing associates. Reject exactly when a fixed class has odd exponent; otherwise form $s$ by the allocation in [F2]. This decision and allocation are complete, including the ramified class and arbitrary multiplicities, by [F2].

Put $e=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$. By [F2], this is a real unit of $R$, positive at both embeddings; [F1] gives $e=\lambda^{2j}$ for an integer $j$. Recover its exponent by multiplying $e$ by $\lambda^{-1}$ while it is at least $\lambda$, or by $\lambda$ while it is below $1$, recording the signed number of multiplications. The resulting unit in $[1,\lambda)$ is $1$ by [F1], so this finds $2j$ exactly, including negative exponents. Set $v=\lambda^j$ and return $t=vs/2^r$. Then $t^\dagger t=v^2s^\dagger s/4^r=\xi$. This also states the actual unit-recovery algorithm; no search over arbitrary coefficients is used.

All rational primes in step 1.1 have $O(L)$ bits, and their multiplicities sum to $O(L)$ since their product is an $O(L)$-bit integer. Each gcd in steps 2.1-2.2 is normalized as in step 1.3, so its output has $O(L)$-bit coefficients. The number of prime generators is at most four per rational prime. A prime in $O$ has integer norm at least two; consequently step 2.3 uses $O(L)$ successful divisions. Products and quotients of at most $O(L)$ such factors have at most $O(L^2)$ coefficient bits: a product in fixed degree adds operand bit lengths plus a constant, and a field inverse is given by the product of the other conjugates divided by the integer norm. Thus $s$, $e$ and the intermediate divisions have polynomial bit length. An element $\lambda^j$ with $B$-bit coefficients has $|j|=O(B)$, because its two real absolute embeddings are $\lambda^j$ and $\lambda^{-j}$ and both are bounded by $2^{O(B)}$. Step 3.1 therefore takes polynomially many bit operations and produces a polynomial-size answer. Modular-root calls are the only randomized operations; their number is $O(L)$ and each has expected polynomial cost by [F3]. This proves the full expected polynomial bit bound, without using the exhaustive factor search in [F1].

For the bounded case, put $\alpha=(\sqrt2)^k\xi=A+B\sqrt2\in R$. Both absolute embeddings of $\alpha$ are at most $2^{k/2}$, so $|A|\le2^{k/2}$ and $|B|\le2^{k/2}/\sqrt2$. If $k$ is even, $\xi=(A+B\sqrt2)/2^{k/2}$; if $k$ is odd, $\xi=(2B+A\sqrt2)/2^{(k+1)/2}$. These expressions and their reductions have $O(k+1)$ coefficient bits. Moreover $|N_R(\alpha)|=2^k\xi\xi^\bullet\le2^k$ is an integer, so the reduced nonzero numerator $n$ is at most $2^k$ (and hence at most $4^k$); its supplied prime factorization has polynomial length in $k+1$. Thus $L$ is polynomial in $k+1$, and step 3.2 yields the asserted bounded-input complexity. For the candidate case, write $u=z/(\sqrt2)^h$ with $z\in O$. Then $(\sqrt2)^{2h}\xi=2^h-z^\dagger z$ is a real element of $O$, hence lies in $R$ by [F1]; the least residual exponent is at most $2h$. Applying the preceding bounds with that exponent proves $n\le4^h$ and expected polynomial cost in $h+1$. Zero was already handled in step 1.1. For unrestricted inputs, real units can have norm one but arbitrarily large coefficients; retaining $L$ in the general statement is therefore necessary.

We calibrate the last bound for $H=h+1\ge1$. The bounded residual lies in $2^{-h}R$, so write $\xi=(a+b\sqrt2)/2^h$ with $|a|,|b|\le2^h$, by adding and subtracting its two embeddings. Using the least clearing exponent of step 1.1 gives $r\le\lceil h/2\rceil$ and $\eta$-coefficient bit lengths at most $h+2$. The input coefficient denominators divide $2^h$. For prime $n=p$, $p\le2^{2h}$; hence its bit length is at most $2h+1$. The cases $n=0,1$ omit these prime calls. At most two real primes and four cyclotomic primes over $p$, together with $\delta$, need be represented. Reusing the modular roots, at most eight modular-root calls and sixteen ring gcds cover steps 2.1-2.2, including harmless duplicate computations. All gcd inputs have coefficient bit lengths at most $8H$: the modular roots are reduced below $p$, and a balanced real factor has coefficients at most $2\sqrt{N_R(p)}=2p$, so converting it to the cyclotomic basis still fits this bound. The real and cyclotomic norm bounds for an integer element with $b$-bit coordinates are respectively $2^{2b+2}$ and $2^{4b+8}$, because each complex embedding has magnitude at most $4\cdot2^b$. Step 1.2 therefore requires fewer than $32(b+2)$ divisions per gcd.

Here is explicit storage and loop bookkeeping for these gcds. Multiplication in the power basis of $O$ has at most four signed product terms per output coefficient, so multiplying elements with coefficient bit lengths $b_1,b_2$ gives lengths at most $b_1+b_2+3$; the real basis obeys the same bound. The other field conjugates only permute or negate coordinates. Forming $x/y$ by multiplying $x$ by the other three conjugates of $y$ and dividing by $N_O(y)$ gives numerator and denominator lengths at most $b_x+3b_y+12$ and $4b_y+12$. Balanced gcd operands have lengths at most $b+6$, by the embedding bounds in step 1.3 and the preceding norm estimate. Thus the unbalanced integer remainder has lengths below $8(b+8)$. Its nonzero embeddings lie between $2^{-8(b+8)-2}$ and $2^{8(b+8)+2}$, by the integer norm and the upper bound for the other embedding. Since $\lambda>2$, balancing needs fewer than $32(b+8)$ unit multiplications, including comparisons; during balancing each embedding stays between its initial and final values, so all coefficient lengths stay below $16(b+8)$. The quotient formulas keep temporary rational coordinates below $512(b+8)$ bits. Allowing eight fixed-degree field actions per balancing iteration and $256$ for division, norm and rounding, $32(b+2)$ divisions, and initial balancing, fewer than $2^{21}(b+8)^2$ field actions suffice per gcd. Here an action means a fixed-degree field multiplication, quotient, norm, sign comparison or coordinate rounding, expanded into integer operations in step 5.3.

For the remaining work, the number of prime factors of $\eta$ counted with multiplicity is at most $\log_2N_O(\eta)\le4h+8\le16H$. Balanced prime-generator coefficients have at most $32H$ bits, including $\delta$. Multiplying at most $16H$ generators gives coefficient lengths below $2^{10}H^2$; successive exact divisions increase length by at most $3(32H)+12$ each by step 5.2, hence stay below $2^{12}H^2$. The quotient $e=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$ has length below $2^{14}H^2$. If $e=\lambda^m$, its two embedding bounds and $\lambda>2$ give $|m|<2^{15}H^2$, so both exponent recovery and construction of $\lambda^{m/2}$ use fewer than $2^{16}H^2$ unit multiplications in total. A unit multiplication increases length by at most three; monotonicity of the embedding sizes during exponent reduction, or the direct power formula during reconstruction, bounds every stored coordinate, including the returned numerator and denominator, by $B=2^{20}H^2$ bits. Sixteen gcds with $b\le8H$, at most $16H$ successful divisions and at most one failed division per generator, at most $25$ associate comparisons, and these unit loops, are together fewer than $2^{40}H^4$ field actions; this also includes reading, denominator clearing, allocation, and checking $t^\dagger t=\xi$ exactly before returning. A field action can be implemented using fewer than $4096$ signed integer operations and rational reductions on values of at most $4096(B+1)$ bits: expand the at most four coordinates, the at most three conjugate factors for inversion, and reduce each rational coordinate by the ordinary integer gcd. Binary schoolbook addition, multiplication and long division of $d$-bit integers take fewer than $2^{10}(d+1)^2$ bit steps, by their nested digit loops. An integer gcd has at most $2d+2$ divisions, since every two Euclidean divisions at least halve its positive divisor. For $d\le4096(B+1)$, $4096$ such integer-gcd costs are below $2^{63}(B+1)^3$. Maintaining the at most four binary array-index counters costs at most $64(B+1)$ further bit operations per digit action, since their lengths are at most $13+\lceil\log_2(B+1)\rceil\le16(B+1)$. Including this overhead and the rational reductions, one field action therefore costs less than $2^{70}(B+1)^4$ bit steps. These bounds deliberately allow more integer operations and bits than any of the displayed fixed-degree formulas require.

Binary powering uses at most $2d$ modular multiplications, and the at most $d$ order-reduction iterations use at most $4d$ modular multiplications each. The schoolbook bounds in step 5.3 consequently put the expected cost of one call below $2^{20}(d+1)^5$ bit steps, including sampling and initialization. Since $d\le2H$, eight calls cost less than $2^{31}H^5$ in expectation. The deterministic part is less than $2^{40}H^4\,2^{70}(2^{20}H^2+1)^4\le2^{194}H^{12}$. Adding the random part gives a bound below $2^{195}H^{12}\le2^{200}H^{20}=P(h)$. For $n=0,1$ the omitted prime calls only reduce the bound. This proves the explicit majorant for the actual chosen arithmetic loops, with no timing assumption about composite inputs.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
